title: The symbiotic and bipolar nebula M 2-9: Morphological variability of the collimated ionized wind arising from the core
question: Investigate the presence and morphological variability of the collimated fast wind and surrounding disk-like dust ring in the central region of the symbiotic and bipolar nebula M 2-9.

what.value: JVLA radio-continuum flux density, size, and SED measurements at 4.86, 8.46, 14.94, and 22.46 GHz, and ~23 GHz image

evidence.quote: We present the $\sim$ 43 GHz image in Fig. 3, with an overlay of the $\sim$ 23 GHz RC emission adapted from (cite: Lim2003).

what.value: Orbital period of 86 years for the binary system

evidence.quote: Although our observations do not have sufficient angular resolution to determine dynamical parameters like the orbital period, we can say that since the time interval between the two observations is around 7 years and taking into account an orbital period of 86 years (cite: Doyle2000; Corradi2011), the angle subtended by the white dwarf in those epochs, as seen from the red giant star, is around 30 degrees.

what.value: SED of M 2-9 for comparison at 345 GHz

evidence.quote: In agreement with (cite: SC2017), and comparing this to the SED presented by them for M2-9 (see their Figure 1), the 345 GHz emission could be a dust ring produced by the WD during its AGB phase (AGB wind; see (cite: Ferrarotti2006; Kwok2000; Kwok1993; Kwok1980) and references therein) in a binary system.

recipe.goal: Calibrate and image JVLA and ALMA continuum observations
recipe.method: Calibrate JVLA data in AIPS including phase self-calibration and image with robust = 0; calibrate ALMA Band 7 data with the ALMA pipeline in CASA and produce continuum maps.
key_parameters: robust weighting parameter of 0 for JVLA Set II

recipe.goal: Compare multi-wavelength and multi-epoch continuum morphologies
recipe.method: Overlay the JVLA ~43 GHz continuum map with the ALMA 345 GHz continuum contours and with the 1999 ~23 GHz JVLA continuum contours to compare the orientation of the jet and dust ring and identify morphological variability between 1999 and 2006.
assumptions: Orbital period of 86 years for the binary system

recipe.goal: Analyze the Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) and source size dependence on frequency
recipe.method: Combine the new ~43 GHz flux density, major/minor axes, and PA measurements with the 4.86-22.46 GHz measurements from Lim & Kwok (2003) to evaluate the spectral indices of flux density and angular size.
assumptions: Isothermal wind with constant expansion velocity (theoretical spectral indices of 0.6 for flux density and -0.7 for angular size from Reynolds 1986)

evidence.quote: We confirm the RC emission from 4.86 to 43.34 GHz as a jet, where the free-free emission is also traced at $\sim$ 43 GHz.

answer_key.quantity: Angle subtended by the white dwarf between 1999 and 2006 epochs

evidence.quote: Although our observations do not have sufficient angular resolution to determine dynamical parameters like the orbital period, we can say that since the time interval between the two observations is around 7 years and taking into account an orbital period of 86 years (cite: Doyle2000; Corradi2011), the angle subtended by the white dwarf in those epochs, as seen from the red giant star, is around 30 degrees.

score_reason: Archival project codes, calibration software versions (CASA 6.1.1.15, pipeline 2020.1.0.40), and calibrator fluxes are clearly stated, and the quantitative JVLA 43 GHz results are tabulated. However, ALMA imaging details are completely omitted, no quantitative ALMA measurements are reported, and there are typographical inconsistencies in the project codes and JVLA frequencies.
rediscovery_reason: Both the JVLA (AL0675) and ALMA (2013.1.00458.S) datasets are public in their respective archives, and the main quantitative results (43 GHz flux density, major/minor axes, PA, and the perpendicular morphology relative to the 345 GHz ring) can be reproduced from standard continuum imaging and 2D Gaussian fitting.
